titles.topic: Periodicity of Chemical Properties of the Elements in Period 3

blocks.text: Reaction of Period 3 elements with oxygen table

blocks.md:
|   | **Chemical equation** | **Reaction conditions** | **Reaction** | **Flame** | **Product** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Na** | 4Na (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2Na<sub>2</sub>O (s) | Heat | Vigorous | Bright yellow | White solid |
| **Mg** | 2Mg (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2MgO (s) | Heat | Vigorous | Bright white | White solid |
| **Al** | 4Al (s) + 3O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (s) | Powdered Al | Fast | Bright white | White powder |
| **Si** | Si (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → SiO<sub>2</sub> (s) | Powdered Si, heat strongly | Slow | Bright white sparkles | White powder |
| **P** | P<sub>4</sub> (s) + 5O<sub>2</sub> (g) → P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> (s) | Heat, excess oxygen | Vigorous | Yellow or white | White clouds |
| **S** | S (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → SO<sub>2</sub> (g) | Powdered S, heat | Gentle | Blue | Toxic fumes |

blocks.label: Exam Hint
blocks.md:
- Textbooks sometimes show the combustion of phosphorus as

  - 4P + 5O<sub>2</sub> → P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>
  - But this shorthand isn’t safe for exams
- Phosphorus exists as P<sub>4</sub> molecules, as stated in the syllabus and mark schemes
- So, you should write reactions with P<sub>4</sub>
- Also, be careful with phosphorus(V) oxide:

  - Examiners expect the molecular formula P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>, not the empirical formula P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>

blocks.text: Reaction of Period 3 elements with chlorine table

blocks.md:
|   | **Chemical equation** | **Reaction conditions** | **Reaction** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Na** | 2Na (s) + Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NaCl (s) | Heat | Vigorous |
| **Mg** | Mg (s) + Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → MgCl<sub>2</sub> (s) | Heat | Vigorous |
| **Al** | 2Al (s) + 3Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub> (s) | Heat | Vigorous |
| **Si** | Si (s) + 2Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → SiCl<sub>4</sub> (l) | Heat | Slow |
| **P** | P<sub>4</sub> (s) + 10Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → 4PCl<sub>5</sub> (s) | Heat, excess chlorine | Slow |
- Sodium reacts **vigorously **with **cold water**:

- The sodium **melts** into a ball and moves across the water surface until it disappears
- **Hydrogen gas** is given off
- The solution formed is **strongly** **alkaline** (pH 14) due to the **sodium hydroxide** which is formed

blocks.text: The reaction of sodium with cold water

blocks.alt: Sodium reacting vigorously with water, producing hydrogen gas and NaOH, making the solution strongly alkaline (pH 14). Chemical equation shown.
blocks.caption: Sodium fizzes while vigorously reacting with water to form sodium hydroxide

blocks.md: - Magnesium reacts **extremely slowly **with cold water:

- The solution formed is **weakly** **alkaline** (pH 9 - 10) as the formed **magnesium hydroxide **is only **slightly soluble**
- When magnesium is **heated**, it reacts **vigorously **with steam (water) to make magnesium oxide and hydrogen gas:

blocks.name: Oxidation Number of Period 3 Oxides & Chlorides

blocks.text: Oxidation Number of Period 3 Oxides & Chlorides

blocks.md:
- Chlorine is more **electronegative **than the other Period 3 elements

  - Therefore, the other Period 3 elements will generally have **positive oxidation states **in their chlorides, while the chlorine has a **negative oxidation state **of -1
- Oxygen is more **electronegative** than any of the Period 3 elements

  - Therefore, the Period 3 elements will have **positive oxidation states **in their oxides, while the oxygen has a **negative oxidation state **of -2

blocks.alt: Periodic table displaying Pauling electronegativity values for elements, including hydrogen (2.1) and fluorine (4.0), with missing values for noble gases.
blocks.caption: The Pauling scale shows that chlorine has a higher electronegativity than the other Period 3 elements and oxygen has a higher electronegativity than all of the Period 3 elements

blocks.text: Oxidation numbers of Period 3 elements in their oxides

blocks.md: - The normal [Oxidation Number Rules](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/chemistry/cie/25/revision-notes/6-electrochemistry/6-1-redox-processes-electron-transfer-and-changes-in-oxidation-number-oxidation-state/oxidation-number-rules/) apply to the Period 3 oxides

blocks.text: Table of formulae of the Period 3 oxides & the elements oxidation numbers

blocks.md:
| **Period 3 element** | **Na** | **Mg** | **Al** | **Si** | **P** | **S** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Formula of oxide** | Na<sub>2</sub>O | MgO | Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> | SiO<sub>2</sub> | P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> | SO<sub>2</sub> SO<sub>3</sub> |
| **Oxidation number of the Period 3 element** | +1 | +2 | +3 | +4 | +5 | +4 +6 |

blocks.label: Exam Hint
blocks.md: - SiO<sub>2</sub> is not written in the specification as expected knowledge but you should be able to apply the oxidation number rules to this and other chemicals

blocks.label: Worked Example
blocks.md:
**Deducing oxidation numbers of Period 3 elements in their oxides**

State the oxidation number of the bold atoms in these compounds or ions.

1. **Na**<sub>2</sub>O
2. **Al**<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>
3. ** P**<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>

**Answer**

1. **Na**<sub>2</sub>O

  - 1 O atom = –2
  - The overall charge of the compound = 0
  - 2 Na atoms = +2
  - Oxidation number of 1 Na atom = (+2) / 2 = +1
2. **Al**<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>

  - 3 O atoms = 3 x (–2) = –6
  - The overall charge of the compound = 0
  - 2 Al atoms = +6
  - Oxidation number of 1 Al atom = (+6) / 2 = +3
3. ** P**<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>

  - 10 O atoms = 10 x (–2) = –20
  - The overall charge of the compound = 0
  - 4 P atoms = +20
  - Oxidation number of 1 P atom = (+20) / 4 = +5

blocks.text: Oxidation numbers of Period 3 elements in their chlorides

blocks.md: - The normal [Oxidation Number Rules](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/chemistry/cie/25/revision-notes/6-electrochemistry/6-1-redox-processes-electron-transfer-and-changes-in-oxidation-number-oxidation-state/oxidation-number-rules/) apply to the Period 3 chlorides

blocks.text: Table of formulae of the Period 3 chlorides & the elements oxidation numbers

blocks.md:
| **Period 3 element** | **Na** | **Mg** | **Al** | **Si** | **P** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Formula of chloride** | NaCl | MgCl<sub>2</sub> | AlCl<sub>3</sub> | SiCl<sub>4</sub> | PCl<sub>5</sub> |
| **Oxidation number of the Period 3 element** | +1 | +2 | +3 | +4 | +5 |

blocks.label: Worked Example
blocks.md:
**Deducing oxidation numbers of Period 3 elements in their chlorides**

State the oxidation number of the bold atoms in these compounds or ions.

1. **Mg**Cl<sub>2</sub>
2. **Al**Cl<sub>3</sub>
3. **P**Cl<sub>5</sub>

**Answer**

1. **Mg**Cl<sub>2</sub>

  - 2 Cl atoms = 2 x (–1) = –2
  - The overall charge of the compound = 0
  - Oxidation number of 1 Mg atom = +2
  - Or, the oxidation number of a Group 2 metal is +2
2. **Al**Cl<sub>3</sub>

  - 3 Cl atoms = 3 x (–1) = –3
  - The overall charge of the compound = 0
  - Oxidation number of 1 Al atom = +3
3. **P**Cl<sub>5</sub>

  - 5 Cl atoms = 5 x (–1) = –5
  - The overall charge of the compound = 0
  - Oxidation number of 1 P atom = +5
- Not all Period 3 oxides **react** with or are **soluble** in water

blocks.text: Reaction of Period 3 oxides with water table

blocks.md:
| **Oxide** | **Chemical equation** | **pH** | **Comments** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Na**<sub>**2**</sub>**O** | Na<sub>2</sub>O (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 2NaOH (aq) | 12 - 14 (Strongly alkaline) | - |
| **MgO** | MgO (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> (aq) | 8 - 10 (Weakly alkaline) | - |
| **Al**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**<sub>**3**</sub> | No reaction | - | Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is insoluble in water |
| **SiO**<sub>**2**</sub> | No reaction | - | SiO<sub>2</sub> is insoluble in water |
| **P**<sub>**4**</sub>**O**<sub>**10**</sub> | P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> (s) + 6H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 4H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> (aq) | 3 - 4 (Weakly acidic) | Vigorous reaction |
| **SO**<sub>**2**</sub> | SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) ⇌ H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub> (aq) | 1 - 2 (Strongly acidic) | - |
| **SO**<sub>**3**</sub> | SO<sub>3</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) | 1 - 2 (Strongly acidic) | - |

blocks.label: Exam Hint
blocks.md:
- Since aluminium oxide does not react or dissolve in water, the oxide layer protects the aluminium metal from corrosion
- Silicon(IV) oxide does not react with water because of its giant covalent structure, so the pH stays at 7
